SPOILERS

How do I loathe Childhood's End? Let me count the ways...

  • humans discover the aliens' home star system by using a Ouija board. Yes, this really happened in Childhood's End.

  • The "Childhood's End" referred to in the title means the death of mankind.

First, all the children turn into severely autistic ferals with psychic powers. Then, they turn into space-ghosts and get devoured by a sort of cosmic superintelligence hive-mind.

Then planet Earth blows up, and everything left on it dies. The End.

And Clarke writes as if this is a good thing. Because, evolution, or something.

This isn't so much a science fiction novel as it is a thoroughly miserable, nihilistic fantasy tale. I don't mind darker themes in sci fi - where would we be without dystopian futurescapes or evil alien invaders or the inevitable robot holocaust? - but I like my fiction to have some sense of heroism, or purpose in it.

There is no purpose in Childhood's End. No heroics. No likeable or memorable characters. Only madness and death.

Clarke wrote some great stories, but there was always something a little bit off-putting about him as a person. Like he was more HAL 9000 than man. His inhuman streak comes to the fore in Childhood's End. There is no swearing, sex, or graphic violence - those things would imply it has some humanity, even of a coarse and wild nature - but its ideas are obscene.

If you think a story where people's children are taken away from them in the worst possible way and the extinction of the human race and the mass destruction of every form of animal and plant life on our planet is described in a curiously bloodless narrative that brings to mind a tired man looking at flies, then you might enjoy Childhood's End.

There is a big difference. Big game publishers today are primarily concerned with little more than profit / time. Consequently if they have reason to believe they can hit their sales targets by releasing today, that's exactly what they're going to do. They cash in the profit and leave a skeleton crew to patch the game together into something playable while the rest of the team is migrated on over to the next project.

However, they're also very risk averse. As much as they want that profit, they don't want to pull the trigger until they're all but certain they can hit their target. Day 1 purchasers are a given, but their quantity isn't. They introduce risk. For instance Activision substantially overestimated the initial demand for Destiny. They were quick to announce that they shipped $500 million of product for day 1 purchase, but went silent once those shelves were stacked but mostly gathering dust, at least relative to their expectations. The company later ended up resorting to announcing sales figures through things like how many player game sessions there were and "registered players" in lieu of actual numbers.

Giving people who value money over quality a way to immediately cash in risk free is a great way of ensuring AAA games continue to be the complete rubbish that they have been for this generation to date.
